extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics; readers of 19th‑century philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of genius madness and art
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical treatise excerpts analyzing the nature, dispositions, somatic conditions, and social reception of genius; the psychological/physical origins of madness; criteria for natural beauty; and the inner nature and epistemic function of the arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius lacks soberness
rubrics_metrics.description: The genius 'lacks soberness', meaning he sees in things more than actually belongs to them, so he is often thrown by trifles into violent emotions incomprehensible to ordinary men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lack of soberness is tied to hyper‑sensibility and vehemence of will; it explains extremes of emotion (grief, joy, fear, anger) and contrasts genius with the 'well‑endowed normal man' who shows 'reasonableness, quiet composure, finished surveyal, certainty and proportionateness of behaviour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyper‑sensibility and passionate vehemence
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is associated with hyper‑sensibility and a vehemence or passionateness of will, physically manifesting as energetic heartbeat and heightened emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This temperament produces extravagance of disposition, quick mood changes (dreamy absentness → passionate excitement), and underlies both creative productivity and personal suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solitude and social incongruity of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius 'lives essentially alone'—too rare and different to be ordinary companionship; his pleasures and interests differ from others'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the intellect predominates over the will, geniuses are morally and personally isolated; they prefer the company of their equals (often via their works) and are poorly adapted to conversation and common thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not adapted for common social thinking or conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellect of the genius is detached from the will and 'not adapted for thinking in common,' producing oppressive superiority that others dislike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently geniuses find more comfort among equals and are often misunderstood or disliked in everyday social interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius favours leisure and production over action
rubrics_metrics.description: The happiest lot for the genius is 'release from action' and leisure for production; action is not the genius's element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genius thrives in conditions allowing uninterrupted creation rather than in active public life; this helps explain biographical patterns of solitary productivity and poor life‑happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of genius are temporally ahead of their age
rubrics_metrics.description: The genius 'comes into his age like a comet'—their course is eccentric and often in contradiction with their contemporaries; their works are flung 'far out on to the way in front' and require time for recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere men of talent align with the spirit of their age and are rewarded quickly; geniuses transcend contemporary apprehension and often receive late recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Somatic condition: predominance of sensibility over irritability and reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: A fundamental somatic condition of genius is an abnormal predominance of sensibility over irritability and reproductive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accounts for the rarity of genius and explains gendered claims in the text (the author asserts this predominance must take place in a male body), and how intellectual overdrive can tax the organism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cerebral isolation from ganglionic (vegetative) system
rubrics_metrics.description: The cerebral system must be 'perfectly separated from the ganglion system by complete isolation', allowing the brain to lead a parasitic, powerful, and independent life on the organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While enabling high intellectual activity, this isolation risks injuring the rest of the organism unless coupled with strong vital constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brain morphology and proportions favouring genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is associated with an unusually developed and massive brain—'especially broad and high'—with relative inferiority of depth, cerebrum preponderant to cerebellum; proportions of white to grey matter have decisive influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Byron's brain weight, Cuvier) are cited; thin spinal cord and nerves and a beautifully arched, thin‑boned skull that does not cramp the brain are also given as favorable anatomical signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental contributions: maternal brain quality and paternal temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius requires both maternal inheritance of brain quality (fine nervous tissue) and paternal contribution of a 'lively, passionate temperament' (energy of the heart and circulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If paternal circulation/temperament is lacking, maternal brain quality yields talent not genius (a phlegmatic intellect); if paternal condition exists without good brain structure it yields vivacity without mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical features aiding cerebral circulation (short stature/neck)
rubrics_metrics.description: Small stature and especially a short neck are favourable because the blood reaches the brain with more force; great minds have seldom large bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the physiological account linking cardiovascular energy to cerebral excitation; exceptions (e.g., Goethe) are acknowledged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childlike character of genius: predominance of intellect over will
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius resembles childhood in that the cerebral/nervous system predominates over other systems; the genius retains the child's predominance of knowing over willing—naïveté and sublime simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This childlike mental plasticity explains early intellectual development, teachability, and the 'big child' quality displayed throughout life in some geniuses (Mozart, Goethe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of youthful intellectuality in geniuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas most people lose the intellectual predominance of youth, 'the chosen' retain a trace of that intellectuality through life; true genius preserves this childlike intellectuality even in old age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sustained predominance of intellect over will permits lifelong creative capacity and distinguishes geniuses from those who become 'grave, sober, thoroughly composed' adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health of mind is perfect recollection
rubrics_metrics.description: The health of the mind 'properly consists in perfect recollection'—the ability to find again in memory every event that was peculiar or significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary forgetting of repetitive events is normal, but inability to recollect specific significant events indicates compromised intellect; credibility as a witness depends on this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Madness defined as a 'broken thread' of memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness is the broken thread of recollection: memory still runs but with decreasing fulness and distinctness, producing gaps which may be filled arbitrarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This model explains delusions: suppression of painful truths (will resisting intellect) leads to gaps, which the intellect then fills, producing false beliefs; believing one's own fabrications is a mark of insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychical origin of madness via will's resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness can arise psychically when the will resists allowing painful or contrary facts to be consciously assimilated by the intellect, preventing proper integration into memory and cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each adverse event must be assimilated into the mental system; when resistance is extreme the operation fails and suppression leads to madness; this provides a principle for distinguishing delusional types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors disproportionately predisposed to madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors are said to become mad proportionally most frequently because they daily assume contradictory parts and strive each evening to forget themselves, misusing memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent role switching and systematic 'forgetting' of identity undermines the integrated course of recollection and paves the way for madness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of psychical and physical causes of madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Madness commonly involves both psychical and physical factors: malformations or disorganisation of the brain or influences from diseased body parts; physical predisposition lowers the external occasion necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical causes often produce hallucinations; the psychical and physical generally intermix (e.g., suicidality often demands both). Early madness may be curable; prolonged states can produce permanent brain changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mania sine delirio (frenzy without insanity) as will unbound
rubrics_metrics.description: A state where the will periodically withdraws entirely from guidance by the intellect, appearing as a blind, impetuous, destructive force—'frenzy without insanity'—in which intuitive knowledge remains though reflective reason is suspended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such attacks the person apprehends and acts upon objects, retains consciousness of present action and later memory, but lacks reflection and consideration; the reason resumes correct function once the attack ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criterion: truth and consistency of nature produces delight
rubrics_metrics.description: The delight in a beautiful landscape arises from the 'perfect truth and consistency of nature'—every modification (foreshortening, concealment, distance, lighting, perspective) is unerringly given to the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the visual brain‑phenomenon of landscape is 'absolutely regular, blameless, and perfect', it sets the whole mind into more correct, purified formal action; a beautiful view is therefore a cathartic of the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence and outline (mountains) contribute to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: The mountain chain's permanence and unchanging outline ('the only constantly permanent line of the landscape') underlies the serious or sublime mood elicited by mountains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not consciously noticed, an obscure feeling of defiance of decay (mountains vs ephemeral human life) is a fundamental note of the sublime feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unforced, uncultivated nature as aesthetically preferable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every spot left free to itself 'decorates at once in the most tasteful manner'—uncultivated, unforced nature displays natural grace and tasteful grouping that art should conceal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underpins the English/Chinese garden principle: hide art so nature appears free; such apparent spontaneity expresses the will of nature and is judged more beautiful than subjective imposition (e.g., formal French gardens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner nature of art: art answers 'What is life?' by perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genuine and successful work of art answers the question 'What is life?' by giving a perceptible image; art speaks the naive, childish language of perception rather than abstract reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each painting, statue, poem, scene, and especially music (more profound) offers a transient, perceptual answer; art provides fragments or examples rather than the universal conceptual answer that philosophy seeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's epistemic status: temporary, perceptual vs philosophical universality
rubrics_metrics.description: Art gives a temporary, not permanent, satisfaction: it furnishes a fragmentary perceptual answer whereas philosophy aims to give a universal, permanent conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating art's success involves whether it convincingly embodies an aspect of life's nature in perceptual form; the limitation (fleeting image) is intrinsic to the arts' mode of expression.
